{"id": "2:180/q39", "question": "What earlier practice occasioned the command?", "turns_on": "whether it responded to showy outsider gifts or broader inheritance customs", "positions": [{"id": "2:180/q39/p1", "position": "The verse redirected showy gifts away from outsiders toward kin", "reasons": "Al-Zajjāj, al-Wāḥidī, al-Aṣamm as reported by Jishumī, and later sources describe pre-Islamic showy gifts to distant people while near kin remained poor. {"id": "2:180/q40", "question": "What did the Prophet leave by way of a will?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:180/q40/p1", "position": "The Prophet left the Book and no inheritable estate or property will", "reasons": "ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · قول غير مسمى: Another view denies that making a will is obligatory, citing al-Nakhaʿi's report that the Prophet died without making one and a hadith that conditions it on wanting to make a will. IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · عبد الله بن أبي أوفى: Asked whether the Prophet made a will, Abdullah ibn Abi Awfa answered no; when asked how the commanded will was fulfilled, he said the Prophet willed the Book of God. | mentions 2:180 IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · ابن عباس: Ibn Kathir likens this to Ibn Abbas’s statement that the Prophet left only what lies between the two covers. {"id": "2:180/q41", "question": "How does this verse connect with surrounding passages?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:180/q41/p1", "position": "The verse follows death and property rulings and prepares the next duties", "reasons": "QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · ابن عباس والحسن: Ibn Abbas and al-Hasan say inheritance shares in Surat al-Nisa abrogated bequests to parents but preserved them for noninheriting relatives; al-Shafi'i and most Malikis agree. | mentions 4:11 QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · ابن عمر وابن عباس وعائشة: The preceding view is also the meaning of reports from Ibn Umar and Aisha and is attributed to Ibn Umar and Ibn Abbas. QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author: Ḥaqqan means due care and assurance, not obligatory duty; limiting it to the Godfearing signals recommendation rather than universal obligation. QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · قيل: One explanation links this to the preceding retaliation ruling: a person facing execution is as though death arrived, so this is time for a bequest. | mentions 2:178 ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author: The will verse follows naturally after the discussion of killing, retaliation, and blood money: it alerts each person to make a will before sudden death. ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · علي: ʿAli stopped a client with seven hundred from making a will, saying that this did not count as wealth under the verse. ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · ابن عطية: Ibn ʿAṭiyya makes kataba govern idha, takes al-waṣiyya as the passive subject, and supplies a response to both conditions from the preceding kataba; Abū Ḥayyān finds this contradictory because idha cannot be both temporal and conditional. ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author: These verses frame the accountable person's life from faith in God at its beginning to the will at death, with major duties and sins selected as examples rather than an exhaustive list. BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · الحرالي: Al-Ḥarālī connects the sequence to graded spiritual education: the preceding passages address those hoping to attain taqwā, then raise the address to what is due of the already pious; the mention of death in retaliation leads to bequest at death. | mentions 2:177, 2:179 DURR-FULL, d. 911 · ابن عباس: Ibn Abbas said this verse had been abrogated while explaining the sura; al-Hakim authenticated the report. ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author: The omitted “O believers” is explained by the recent admonition, the link to the preceding discussion of the dead, or the ruling’s lack of hardship. ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author: The wording is contrasted with the same “written upon you” formula for retaliation at 2:178. | mentions 2:178"}, {"id": "2:180/q41/p2", "position": "This fuller bequest verse preceded fixed inheritance shares", "reasons": "QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author: This verse is fuller than the other Qur'anic mentions and preceded the fixed inheritance shares."}, {"id": "2:180/q41/p3", "position": "The sequence traces life from faith to bequest at death", "reasons": "ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author: These verses frame the accountable person's life from faith in God at its beginning to the will at death, with major duties and sins selected as examples rather than an exhaustive list."}, {"id": "2:180/q41/p4", "position": "Inheritance shares later included women and fixed quotas", "reasons": "KURANYOLU-TEFSIR · author: The inheritance passage in Nisa included female relatives among heirs and, with related verses and hadiths, set fixed, unalterable inheritance shares. | mentions 4:11"}, {"id": "2:180/q41/p5", "position": "Bequest is also mentioned in the inheritance and witnessing verses", "reasons": "STUDYQURAN · author: The term bequest is also used in 4:12 and 5:106. | mentions 4:12, 5:106"}]}
{"id": "2:180/q42", "question": "What inward applications are drawn from this passage?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:180/q42/p1", "position": "Spiritual fatherhood can outweigh worldly patronage", "reasons": "QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author: Al-Qurtubi suggests Abu al-Aliyah favored Banu Hashim because he studied with Ibn Abbas; spiritual fatherhood outweighed his freedwoman's worldly emancipation."}, {"id": "2:180/q42/p2", "position": "The sequence advances believers toward and within piety", "reasons": "BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · الحرالي: Al-Ḥarālī connects the sequence to graded spiritual education: the preceding passages address those hoping to attain taqwā, then raise the address to what is due of the already pious; the mention of death in retaliation leads to bequest at death. | mentions 2:177, 2:179"}, {"id": "2:180/q42/p3", "position": "Death invites discipline that enlivens the heart", "reasons": "BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author: The Persian lines value freedom and death as a passage to greater life; the wise should subdue the self through spiritual discipline and enliven the heart with abiding life."}, {"id": "2:180/q42/p4", "position": "The Prophet and his descendants are beneficiaries as allies", "reasons": "TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author: The author links the bequest to 33:6: early inheritance through brotherhood was replaced by kinship, while a good deed to allies remained; the Prophet and his purified descendants count as allies, making this bequest the exception. | mentions 33:6"}, {"id": "2:180/q42/p5", "position": "A sixth to a third is a right for the possessor of the matter", "reasons": "TABATABAI, d. 1402 · الصادق عليه السلام: Al-Sadiq describes a right placed by God in people’s wealth for ‘the possessor of this matter,’ bounded from one-sixth to one-third; al-Saduq also transmits this in al-Faqih."}]}
{"id": "2:180/q43", "question": "What principles about transmitted readings are mentioned?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:180/q43/p1", "position": "Performance and pronunciation can vary within the codex", "reasons": "IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author: Early reciters in regions with Uthman’s codices read in local dialects; variation concerned performance forms, not added or omitted letters or readings against the codex’s grammar. {"id": "2:180/q44", "question": "How is Qurʾānic composition discussed alongside this material?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:180/q44/p1", "position": "Inimitability lies in grammatical composition rather than isolated words", "reasons": "BINTSHATI-IJAZ, d. 1419 · author: Al-Baqillani left later inimitability writers a rich rhetorical vocabulary; the Sakaki school inherited his method of placing Qur'anic examples beside human speech without distinction. {"id": "2:185/q01", "question": "What does shahr mean and why is it so called?", "turns_on": "Whether the root points to public visibility, the crescent, or the measured lunar period.", "positions": [{"id": "2:185/q01/p1", "position": "A month is the publicly visible or known lunar interval.", "reasons": "Al-Tabari invokes the drawn sword and appearing crescent; al-Wahidi notes debts and rituals timed by months; Ibn Ashur cites the twelve-month year in 9:36."}, {"id": "2:185/q01/p2", "position": "Shahr may itself denote the visible new crescent.", "reasons": "Al-Zajjaj and Dhu al-Rumma's verse call the crescent shahr; Abu Hayyan describes its public appearance."}]}
{"id": "2:185/q02", "question": "Why is the month named Ramadan?", "turns_on": "Which suggested root or image explains the name.", "positions": [{"id": "2:185/q02/p1", "position": "It was named for scorching heat, hot stones, or the season of its naming.", "reasons": "Al-Tabari's Arab-language authority cites scorched camel feet; Baghawi prefers this root; Ibn Atiyya notes former name Nathir. {"id": "2:185/q03", "question": "Is Ramadan a divine name, and may the month be called Ramadan alone?", "turns_on": "Authority of the divine-name report and authenticated bare usage.", "positions": [{"id": "2:185/q03/p1", "position": "Ramadan is a divine name, so one should say 'month of Ramadan'.", "reasons": "Mujahid and a reported Prophetic prohibition give this reason."}, {"id": "2:185/q03/p2", "position": "Ramadan alone is permitted as the month's name.", "reasons": "Ibn Abbas and Zayd allowed it; Qurtubi cites sound bare usage, and Ibn Kathir says the prohibition route through Abu Ma'shar and his son is weak or abandoned."}]}
{"id": "2:185/q04", "question": "What duration and recurrence does the named month denote?", "turns_on": "Lunar sighting versus a fixed thirty-day month, and whether each annual Ramadan is included.", "positions": [{"id": "2:185/q04/p1", "position": "It is a recurring lunar month of twenty-nine or thirty days.", "reasons": "Al-Harali describes one appearance of the moon to the next; Ibn Ashur says the recurring name renews the fast annually; the Prophet's report explicitly allows twenty-nine days."}, {"id": "2:185/q04/p2", "position": "It must always be a full thirty days.", "reasons": "Al-Sadiq says the Prophet always completed thirty; Tabrisi answers that a completed lunar count can be twenty-nine or thirty."}]}
{"id": "2:185/q05", "question": "How is 'month of Ramadan' construed grammatically?", "turns_on": "Whether the nominative opens a clause, supplies an omitted subject or predicate, or apposes the earlier fasting phrase; the accusative has its own parses.", "positions": [{"id": "2:185/q05/p1", "position": "Nominative: it explains the earlier counted days as Ramadan, often by an omitted subject.", "reasons": "Al-Akhfash, al-Tabari, al-Farra and Ibn Ashur link it to 2:184; Ibn Ashur rejects a disconnected new subject."}, {"id": "2:185/q05/p2", "position": "Nominative: it is a subject whose predicate is the revelation clause or the fasting command.", "reasons": "Al-Zajjaj and others permit the relative clause; al-Wahidi and Abu Ali prefer making that clause an adjective so the command supplies the predicate and the fast becomes explicit."}, {"id": "2:185/q05/p3", "position": "Nominative: it apposes the prior fasting obligation.", "reasons": "Al-Kisai supplies fasting Ramadan; Abu Hayyan and al-Samin object to the distance and reversed inclusion apposition, though an omitted siyam can rescue it."}, {"id": "2:185/q05/p4", "position": "Accusative: an omitted imperative exhorts people to fast Ramadan.", "reasons": "Al-Samin prefers 'fast the month'; Abu Ubayd also favors the imperative, though al-Nahhas calls it remote because Ramadan was not previously named."}, {"id": "2:185/q05/p5", "position": "Accusative: it apposes the counted days or functions as a time adverb.", "reasons": "Al-Akhfash, al-Rummani and others link it to 2:184; al-Akhfash also allows fasting during Ramadan. The long separation is noted."}, {"id": "2:185/q05/p6", "position": "Accusative: it is governed by the prior 'that you fast' or 'fasting'.", "reasons": "Al-Kisai and al-Kashshaf propose it; al-Nahhas and Abu Hayyan reject splitting the relative construction from its antecedent."}]}
{"id": "2:185/q06", "question": "How is shahr Ramadan pronounced or read?", "turns_on": "Case of shahr and assimilation or transfer between the two r sounds.", "positions": [{"id": "2:185/q06/p1", "position": "The common reading gives shahr the nominative.", "reasons": "Al-Zajjaj calls this more common; al-Nahhas names the readers of the accusative."}, {"id": "2:185/q06/p2", "position": "Mujahid, Shahr ibn Hawshab, and others read shahr accusative.", "reasons": "The accusative supports imperative, apposition, or adverbial analyses."}, {"id": "2:185/q06/p3", "position": "Abu Amr and others assimilate the adjacent r sounds.", "reasons": "Al-Nahhas objects that two quiescent consonants meet; Kufans transfer the vowel to ha, and Abu Hayyan and al-Samin prioritize sound transmission over analogy."}]}

{"id": "2:185/q08", "question": "What is the name Qur'an derived from?", "turns_on": "Proper name versus recitation, gathering, joining, corroborating signs, or utterance.", "positions": [{"id": "2:185/q08/p1", "position": "It is a proper, un-derived name for God's Book.", "reasons": "Al-Shafi'i compares Torah and Gospel; Qurtubi favors derivation."}, {"id": "2:185/q08/p2", "position": "It derives from reciting and originally means recitation.", "reasons": "Razi and Qurtubi cite poetry and 17:78; the verbal noun came to name the recited speech."}, {"id": "2:185/q08/p3", "position": "It derives from gathering or joining its parts and teachings.", "reasons": "Baghawi cites the idiom of gathering water; Razi and Abu Hayyan distinguish qara'a and qarana derivations, while Abu Hayyan rejects the water-root argument."}, {"id": "2:185/q08/p4", "position": "It derives from qarā'in, mutually corroborating signs.", "reasons": "Al-Farra cites 4:82: a nondivine book would contain contradictions."}, {"id": "2:185/q08/p5", "position": "It names what the reciter casts from the mouth.", "reasons": "Qutrub compares a camel expelling afterbirth."}]}
{"id": "2:185/q09", "question": "How is al-Qur'an read with respect to hamza?", "turns_on": "Unhamzated lexical origin versus phonetic transfer and deletion.", "positions": [{"id": "2:185/q09/p1", "position": "Ibn Kathir reads it without hamza; many others pronounce hamza.", "reasons": "Al-Farisi and later sources report the distributions; Abu Hayyan and al-Samin prefer transferred hamza vowel and deletion over a separate q-r-n root."}, {"id": "2:185/q09/p2", "position": "The unhamzated form can reflect q-r-n, joining.", "reasons": "Some grammarians treat its nun as original and link it to the joined suras and verses."}]}
{"id": "2:185/q10", "question": "In what sense did the Qur'an descend in Ramadan?", "turns_on": "A complete heavenly descent, annual installments, the start of revelation, revelation concerning Ramadan, or a single descent of an underlying reality.", "positions": [{"id": "2:185/q10/p1", "position": "The whole Qur'an descended at once to the lowest heaven, then gradually to Muhammad.", "reasons": "Ibn Abbas places it in Bayt al-Izza on Laylat al-Qadr; reports vary twenty, twenty-one, and twenty-three years and the destination's name. Razi prefers this because inzal suggests one descent; Qurtubi calls it consensus."}, {"id": "2:185/q10/p2", "position": "Each year's destined portion descended on its Night of Decree, then reached Muhammad as needed.", "reasons": "Ibn Jurayj places each year's share with Gabriel in the lowest heaven; Muqatil, al-Halimi and al-Mawardi are cited for multi-year nights."}, {"id": "2:185/q10/p3", "position": "The Qur'an's revelation to Muhammad began in Ramadan.", "reasons": "Ibn Ishaq treats the first portion as the whole; Razi considers this figurative; Elmalili prefers the Hira beginning, while Tabatabai objects that the mission began in Rajab."}, {"id": "2:185/q10/p4", "position": "The wording refers to revelation about Ramadan's fasting duty or merit.", "reasons": "Mujahid and al-Dahhak identify 2:183 or the duty; Sufyan ibn Uyayna and al-Husayn ibn al-Fadl identify its virtue. Ibn Kathir calls this strange."}, {"id": "2:185/q10/p5", "position": "Gabriel reviewed the already revealed Qur'an with Muhammad during Ramadan.", "reasons": "Al-Sha'bi says God confirmed or erased what He willed during the review."}, {"id": "2:185/q10/p6", "position": "The undivided reality of the Book descended to Muhammad's heart at once; detailed speech descended over time.", "reasons": "Tabatabai argues from 43:1-4, 56:75-80 and 11:1 that detailed verses are the image of the guarded original; event-specific address and abrogation could not pre-exist as speech."}]}
{"id": "2:185/q11", "question": "What dates do reports give for scriptures revealed in Ramadan?", "turns_on": "The reported day and scripture sequence differ.", "positions": [{"id": "2:185/q11/p1", "position": "Scrolls first, Torah sixth, Gospel thirteenth, Qur'an twenty-fourth.", "reasons": "Prophetic chronologies from Wathila and others; some add Psalms on the eighteenth."}, {"id": "2:185/q11/p2", "position": "Scrolls third, Torah sixth, Gospel thirteenth or eighteenth, Qur'an twenty-fourth.", "reasons": "Abu Dharr's variant has scrolls third and, in one version, Gospel eighteenth; Abu Hayyan says the variants might mark beginning and completion."}, {"id": "2:185/q11/p3", "position": "Psalms twelfth and Gospel eighteenth, with Qur'an twenty-fourth.", "reasons": "Jabir's chronology interchanges dates found in the Wathila reports."}, {"id": "2:185/q11/p4", "position": "Gospel twelfth and Psalms eighteenth, with Qur'an twenty-fourth.", "reasons": "Aisha's chronology differs from both Jabir and Wathila."}, {"id": "2:185/q11/p5", "position": "Qur'an twenty-third, with scrolls first, Torah sixth and Psalms eighteenth.", "reasons": "The chronology attributed to the Prophet in Tabatabai gives the Qur'an a different night."}]}
{"id": "2:185/q12", "question": "What does the verse establish about Laylat al-Qadr?", "turns_on": "The conjunction of Ramadan with 97:1 and 44:3, and the reported dates of the night.", "positions": [{"id": "2:185/q12/p1", "position": "Laylat al-Qadr is a Ramadan night, identified with the blessed night.", "reasons": "Ibn Umar infers this from 2:185 and 97:1; Qurtubi links 44:3."}, {"id": "2:185/q12/p2", "position": "Some reports identify it as Ramadan's twenty-fourth night.", "reasons": "Ibn Abbas's descent reports and al-Hasan's reading of Wathila's chronology support this; other reports place the Qur'an at mid-Ramadan or the twenty-third."}]}
{"id": "2:185/q13", "question": "How does the Qur'an guide people here?", "turns_on": "General direction, a restricted audience, or inward illumination.", "positions": [{"id": "2:185/q13/p1", "position": "It guides people toward truth, right action, and God's pleasure.", "reasons": "Muqatil and Tabari describe religious direction; Ibn Ashur adds public and private interests; Ibn Kathir says believers benefit through faith and reflection."}, {"id": "2:185/q13/p2", "position": "It guides ordinary people generally, while clear proofs address those mature in knowledge.", "reasons": "Tabatabai argues ordinary people need an explaining guide whereas the learned can distinguish truth through signs."}, {"id": "2:185/q13/p3", "position": "Its intelligibility itself refutes claims that faith or an Imam alone supplies understanding.", "reasons": "Jishumi says guidance would add nothing if knowledge were necessary or apparent meanings inaccessible."}]}
{"id": "2:185/q14", "question": "What are the clear signs of guidance?", "turns_on": "Legal clarifications, theological proofs, earlier history, or experienced insight.", "positions": [{"id": "2:185/q14/p1", "position": "They explain lawful and unlawful matters, limits, duties, and judgments.", "reasons": "Al-Tabari, al-Suddi and many later commentators list legal rulings."}, {"id": "2:185/q14/p2", "position": "They are clear arguments for divine oneness and the Messenger's truth.", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur singles out less visible guidance contested by many; Baydawi includes inimitability."}, {"id": "2:185/q14/p3", "position": "They include prophetic stories, prior laws, histories, and decisive admonitions.", "reasons": "Al-Asamm and al-Qadi distinguish this from initial knowledge; Ibn Atiyya also lists decisive verses and admonitions."}, {"id": "2:185/q14/p4", "position": "They are inward signs disclosed to the fasting person.", "reasons": "Al-Harali names an illuminated heart, humbled soul and prepared thought."}]}
{"id": "2:185/q15", "question": "What is al-Furqan in this phrase?", "turns_on": "Criterion of truth, legal decisiveness, the Torah, or escape from doubt.", "positions": [{"id": "2:185/q15/p1", "position": "It distinguishes truth from falsehood.", "reasons": "Tabari and the majority give this gloss; Abu Hayyan notes its cadence with adjacent endings."}, {"id": "2:185/q15/p2", "position": "It denotes decisive rulings within the Qur'an that must be followed.", "reasons": "Abu Abd Allah distinguishes the whole book from its binding clear judgments."}, {"id": "2:185/q15/p3", "position": "It denotes the Torah.", "reasons": "Abu Salih gives this identification."}, {"id": "2:185/q15/p4", "position": "It is a way out of religious doubt and error.", "reasons": "Muqatil and Ibn al-Jawzi point to 3:4 and 8:29."}]}
